items.title: Success Profiles
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Success Profiles is the framework the Civil Service uses to describe a job and to choose the right person. It has five elements: Behaviours (the actions and activities a person does that show how they work), Strengths (the things a person does well and enjoys, which give them energy), Ability (the aptitude or potential to do the job, often measured with tests), Technical (the specific professional skills or qualifications needed) and Experience (the knowledge and background gained in previous activities, paid or unpaid). A particular job uses some of the five, not always all of them. The advert tells you which. A good application shows each requirement with a specific example rather than general claims.

questions.prompt: How many elements are there in the Civil Service Success Profiles?
Which of these is one of the five Success Profiles elements?
How do Strengths differ from Behaviours?

options.text: They mean exactly the same thing
Strengths are what you do well and enjoy, while Behaviours are the actions you take at work

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a behaviour question and a strengths question in an interview, and how you would prepare differently for each.
questions.answer: A behaviour question asks for evidence from your past, for example 'tell us about a time when you ...', so you prepare specific examples in advance, structured with STAR. A strengths question asks what you enjoy and are good at, often with quick, open questions such as 'what do you do on a day when everything goes wrong?', so there is no single right answer and being natural and honest matters more than rehearsed scripts. Prepare by knowing your own strengths and reading the role, but do not memorise answers.
questions.rubric: Should say behaviour = past examples, prepared with STAR; strengths = natural, energising, quick, less rehearsed. Should give a different preparation for each.

items.title: The Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: There are nine Civil Service Behaviours: Seeing the Big Picture, Changing and Improving, Making Effective Decisions, Leadership, Communicating and Influencing, Working Together, Developing Self and Others, Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace. Each is described at several levels, from the entry grades up to the Senior Civil Service, and an advert tells you which behaviours are tested for the role and at what level. For entry grades the descriptions are about everyday things: listening and being clear, helping colleagues, following procedures accurately, spotting what could work better, taking responsibility for your own work and meeting deadlines. Learn the behaviours listed in your advert and for each think of two or three examples from your life.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Civil Service Behaviour?
What is the core idea of the behaviour Delivering at Pace?

options.text: Taking responsibility for delivering well-organised outcomes on time and with energy
Working faster than anyone else, whatever the quality

questions.prompt: You changed how a playgroup rota is organised so that fewer parents were left out and it took less time. Which behaviour is this best evidence for?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture of government finance

questions.prompt: Choose three behaviours and, for each, name an example from home life, volunteering or community activity that you could use as evidence. Explain briefly how it shows the behaviour.
questions.answer: A good answer picks three behaviours and pairs each with a real example, for instance: Working Together, from a school fundraising committee where the writer helped five volunteers agree roles and share tasks; Managing a Quality Service, from keeping a household or a rota accurate, on time and fair to everyone; Communicating and Influencing, from persuading a group or professional, for example writing a clear letter to the council or school and getting a result. Each example states what the person did, how it showed the behaviour and what the result was.
questions.rubric: Should name three behaviours, give plausible real-life examples (not invented jargon), and explain how each shows the behaviour with action and result.

items.title: Building an answer with STAR
items.body: STAR is a simple way to structure an example. Situation: set the scene briefly. Task: say what you were responsible for or trying to achieve. Action: describe what you personally did, step by step. Result: say what happened and what you learned. Spend most of your answer on the Action. Say 'I' rather than 'we', because the assessor is scoring you, not the group. Use real detail: numbers, dates, people, outcomes. A strong answer is specific and honest. A weak answer is vague ('we organised an event and it went well') or only describes the situation. Write your examples down in advance, check the result is clear, and match each example to the behaviours the advert asks for.

questions.prompt: Which part of a STAR answer should be the longest?

options.text: Task: the title of the role
'I contacted six families, agreed a rota and cut missed pickups from four a month to none.'
'We did a rota and it went fine.'
'The group sorted it out in the end.'
'It was a very busy time for everyone.'

questions.prompt: Rewrite this weak answer using STAR: 'We organised a charity coffee morning and it went well.' Make up realistic details.
questions.answer: For example: Situation: our local primary school needed money for books. Task: I volunteered to lead a coffee morning to raise £300. Action: I asked three local shops for donations, booked the hall, created a rota for eight volunteers, wrote and sent invitations and managed the cash on the day. Result: we raised £420, 40% more than the target, and the school asked me to run it again next term. A good answer uses 'I', gives specifics and ends with a clear result.
questions.rubric: Should include all four STAR parts, personal actions using I, concrete details and a measurable result.

items.title: Using unpaid and home experience as evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: The Experience and Behaviours elements are about what you have done, paid or unpaid. Running a household, caring for children or relatives, volunteering, helping at a school, serving on a committee, organising a community event or managing a family budget all build skills that the Civil Service values: planning, organising, communicating, solving problems, handling money, keeping records, supporting others under pressure. Describe them in the language of work and not in apologies. Say 'I managed the household budget of £2,000 a month' rather than 'I'm just a housewife'. Be honest, be specific and give a result. Do not invent or exaggerate, because assessors test examples with follow-up questions.

questions.prompt: Can unpaid experience such as volunteering or caring count as evidence in an application?

options.text: Yes, if it shows the skills and behaviours the job asks for
Only if it lasted ten years
Only if the employer was a government department

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest piece of evidence?

options.text: A list of adjectives about yourself
A statement that you are hard-working
A specific example with what you did and the result

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes household budgeting best in a job application?

options.text: 'I'm only a housewife so I look after the money a bit.'
'Money matters are usually left to me.'
'I spend most of my time at home.'
'I plan and track our monthly budget, compared suppliers and cut our food bill by 15% without cutting meals.'

questions.prompt: You have not had paid work for eight years. Draft two or three sentences to introduce yourself at the start of a personal statement.
questions.answer: A good example: 'I am returning to work after eight years as a full-time parent, during which I managed a household budget, coordinated school and community activities and served as a volunteer treasurer for a local group. These roles built my skills in planning, accuracy and communicating with people from different backgrounds, which I now want to use in an Administrative Officer role.' It is honest, positive, specific, mentions skills from the advert and does not apologise.
questions.rubric: Should be honest about the break, name specific roles and skills, link to the role, and avoid apologising or demeaning language.
